analysis.one_liner: Banned Japanese car imports for five years and taxed automakers' profits unless reinvested.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban Japanese car imports for five years and tax automakers' profits was introduced by one representative and three cosponsors and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban imports of cars from Japan—and cars made by Japanese-owned plants anywhere outside Japan—for 1996 through 2000, and require that cars sold in the U.S. be built with all-American parts. It would also impose a 100% tax on profits Japanese-owned U.S. plants send back to Japan, tax domestic automakers for spending profits on anything besides research, retooling, or retraining (including wage and dividend increases above inflation), and deny tax deductions for executive pay more than 25 times the lowest-paid employee. It never advanced past the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. auto manufacturers and parts suppliers, who would be protected from Japanese competition for five years and gain market share as imports disappear; auto assembly and parts workers whose jobs would be more secure; the bill also pressures automakers to reinvest profits rather than pay them out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. automakers, parts suppliers, and auto workers

how_it_helps.text: It bans all imports of Japanese vehicles—and vehicles made abroad by Japanese-owned companies—for five years, pushing buyers toward cars built in the U.S. [S2] [S3]
It requires that cars sold in the U.S. by American manufacturers (and Japanese-owned U.S. plants) be made entirely of U.S.-produced parts, protecting domestic parts makers. [S2] [S3]
It taxes Japanese-owned U.S. plants at 100% on any profits they transfer to Japan, keeping that money from leaving the country. [S2] [S3]

It taxes domestic automakers at 100% on profits spent on anything besides research and development, retooling factories, or retraining workers, and denies tax deductions for executive compensation exceeding 25 times the lowest-paid employee's pay. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Car buyers, who would face higher prices and fewer choices during the import ban; consumers generally, since the all-U.S.-parts rule would raise production costs; and U.S. exporters in other industries, who risk retaliation from Japan and other trading partners.

drawbacks.text: Banning imports for five years would likely raise car prices and shrink the choices available to buyers, since fewer vehicles would be for sale. [S2] [S3]
The 100% tax on domestic automakers applies to wage increases above inflation, which directly limits how much autoworkers' pay could rise during the period. [S3]

A sweeping import ban and domestic-content mandate would almost certainly provoke retaliation against U.S. exports and conflict with U.S. trade commitments, endangering jobs in other export industries.

The all-U.S.-parts requirement makes selling a car unlawful unless every specified part is domestically produced, with a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per day of violation—an enforcement regime that could raise costs even for compliant manufacturers. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real 1992 concern—auto plant closures and job losses—as Japanese-owned plants were gaining share of the U.S. market. But its main tool, a five-year import ban plus an all-U.S.-parts rule, works by making cars more expensive for buyers and inviting trade retaliation, and its profit-reinvestment tax even caps autoworker wage growth above inflation. The executive-pay ratio cap and the reinvestment mandate are more defensible ideas, but the package as a whole trades broad consumer costs for protection of one industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to the Trade subcommittee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. William Lipinski introduced the Rebuild the American Automobile Industry Act on February 5, 1992, with three Democratic cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
The House referred it jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees the day it was introduced. [S5]
On February 13, 1992, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade, which is the last recorded action on the bill. [S5]
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died without ever reaching the House floor. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Car buyers and importers of foreign vehicles are better off, since no import ban or domestic-parts mandate ever took effect; U.S. automakers gained nothing from the bill's death, but also faced no new taxes on their profits or executive pay.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the bill's four sponsors and cosponsors were all Democrats, and the record shows no Republican position and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Japanese automakers and their overseas plants
industries.note: The bill bans their vehicles from the U.S. market for five years and taxes at 100% any profits their U.S. plants send to Japan. Keeping their cars on sale would have meant lower prices and more choices for car buyers, so their interest in defeating the bill ran alongside consumers'. [S2] [S3]

The import ban and all-U.S.-parts mandate would hand them a protected market and lock in their role at buyers' expense, but the bill also taxes them at 100% for spending profits on dividends, wages above inflation, or anything besides research, retooling, or retraining, and denies deductions for executive pay over 25 times the lowest-paid worker. [S2] [S3]
A five-year import ban plus a requirement that every part be U.S.-made would reduce the supply of vehicles and raise prices for anyone shopping for a car. [S2] [S3]
